claim: Act5C forms the cortical actin network in the Drosophila larval fat body.
source: We find Act5C localizes to the FB cell surface and cell-cell boundaries, where it intimately contacts peripheral LDs (pLDs), forming a cortical actin network for cell architectural support.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing Act5C localization and RNAi depletion experiments demonstrating loss of cortical actin network upon Act5C knockdown.

claim: FB-specific loss of Act5C perturbs FB triglyceride (TG) storage and LD morphology.
source: FB-specific loss of Act5C perturbs FB triglyceride (TG) storage and LD morphology, resulting in developmentally delayed larvae that fail to develop into flies.
evidence: The claim is supported by TG measurements and LD imaging data comparing control and Act5C-depleted larvae.

claim: Act5C-deficient larvae display blunted insulin signaling and reduced feeding.
source: In line with this, Act5C-deficient larvae display blunted insulin signaling and reduced feeding.
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data showing reduced Tobi expression, tGPH reporter assays showing reduced PIP3 signaling, and feeding assays showing reduced food intake.

claim: Act5C is required for Lpp secretion from the FB for lipid transport.
source: Mechanistically, we also show this diminished signaling correlates with decreased lipophorin (Lpp) lipoprotein-mediated lipid trafficking, and find Act5C is required for Lpp secretion from the FB for lipid transport.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and TEM data showing intracellular Lpp accumulation in Act5C-depleted FBs, western blot data showing reduced hemolymph Lpp, and gut lipid accumulation data.

claim: Most F-actin in the fat body is highly polarized to FB cell surfaces exposed to the hemolymph and intra-tissue cell-cell boundaries.
source: We found that most F-actin was highly polarized to FB cell surfaces exposed to the hemolymph, as well as intra-tissue cell-cell boundaries, with a dim intracellular pool also detectable (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images showing phalloidin-stained F-actin distribution in FB tissue.

claim: The cortical F-actin localizes to microridge protrusions at the tissue surface, giving the FB surface a 'foamy' appearance.
source: Imaging revealed that the cortical F-actin localized to microridge protrusions at the tissue surface, giving the FB surface a 'foamy' appearance consistent with previous reports showing the plasma membrane of FB cells is densely ruffled (Diaconeasa et al., 2013; Ugrankar et al., 2019, Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data and is consistent with previously published reports.

claim: The cortical actin network appears to intimately encircle many peripheral LDs (pLDs) adjacent to the cell surface.
source: Z-section confocal microscopy of FBs stained with the fluorescent F-actin dye Cell Mask Actin Tracking Stain, together with LD dye monodansylpentane (MDH), revealed a bright ruffled cortical F-actin cytoskeleton that appeared to intimately encircle many pLDs adjacent to the cell surface (Figure 1B, red arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images showing co-localization of F-actin and pLDs.

claim: In the tissue interior, the actin network does not encircle individual medial LDs (mLDs), but rather localizes along cell edges at cell-cell boundaries.
source: In contrast, in the tissue interior the actin network did not encircle individual mLDs, but rather localized along cell edges at cell-cell boundaries.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy observations of actin distribution in the tissue mid-plane.

claim: Targeted RNAi depletion of Act5C, but not any other actin isoforms, dramatically altered F-Actin polarization to cell surfaces and cell-cell boundaries.
source: Strikingly, targeted RNAi depletion indicated that Act5C (Dcg-Gal4 >UAS-Act5CRNAi), but not any other actin isoforms, dramatically altered F-Actin polarization to cell surfaces and cell-cell boundaries (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by phalloidin staining and confocal imaging of FBs with RNAi depletion of different actin isoforms.

claim: Act5C is necessary for the 'foamy' surface appearance of FB cells.
source: Additionally, the FB cell surface now appeared smooth and lacked its microridge patterning, suggesting Act5C, but not other actin isoforms, was required for this 'foamy' surface appearance (Figure 1C, red boxes are single FB cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging showing loss of microridge patterning in Act5C-depleted FBs.

claim: Act5C mRNA is reduced by approximately 70% in Act5CRNAi FBs.
source: To confirm that loss of the FB cortical F-actin network was specifically due to depletion of the Act5C isoform, we utilized quantitative PCR (QPCR) to confirm an ~70% knockdown of Act5C mRNA with our TRiP UAS-Act5CRNAi line (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data measuring Act5C mRNA levels.

claim: Dcg-Gal4 is a FB-specific driver.
source: We detected GFP signal only in the FB but not in other tissues, validating Dcg-Gal4 as a FB-specific driver, as previously reported (Suh et al., 2008; Ugrankar et al., 2015, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP expression data in different tissues and is consistent with previously published reports.

claim: Two additional independent UAS-RNAi lines for Act5C recapitulated the initial observed Act5CRNAi phenotype.
source: To rule out off-target effects from the Bloomington TRiP Act5CRNAi line, we tested two additional independent UAS-RNAi lines for Act5C obtained from the Vienna Drosophila Research Center (Act5CRNAi VDRC#7139, Act5CRNAi VDRC#101438) using the Cg-Gal4 FB driver. Both recapitulated the initial observed Act5CRNAi phenotype, similarly ablating the cortical actin network (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging of FBs with two independent RNAi lines showing similar phenotypes.

claim: The TRiP Act5CRNAi line specifically targets only the Act5C isoform and not other actin isoforms.
source: Thus, none of the other ActXX-GFP proteins appeared to be impacted by Act5CRNAi, indicating that the TRiP Act5CRNAi line specifically targeted only the Act5C isoform (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-expression experiments showing that other GFP-tagged actins localize normally in Act5CRNAi FBs.

claim: Act5C-GFP decorates FB cell surfaces and enriches at cell-cell interfaces.
source: Analogous to the phalloidin and Cell Mask Actin staining of wildtype fat tissue, Act5C-GFP decorated FB cell surfaces and enriched at cell-cell interfaces (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging of Act5C-GFP expressing FBs.

claim: Act5C-GFP intimately wraps around pLDs at the cell periphery.
source: Act5C-GFP also intimately wrapped around pLDs at the cell periphery (Figure 1D, red arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging showing Act5C-GFP localization around pLDs.

claim: The Act5C-RFP cortical actin network and plasma membrane are closely overlaid.
source: This revealed that the Act5C-RFP cortical actin network and PM are closely overlaid, and both exhibit the microridge pattern intimately encircling pLDs (Figure 1E, red arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging of FBs co-expressing Act5C-RFP and mCD8-GFP plasma membrane marker.

claim: Act5C loss significantly increased the average size of pLDs.
source: Specifically, Act5C loss significantly increased the average size of pLDs, but drastically reduced the average size of mLDs (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of LD sizes in confocal images of control and Act5C-depleted FBs.

claim: Act5C loss drastically reduced the average size of mLDs.
source: Specifically, Act5C loss significantly increased the average size of pLDs, but drastically reduced the average size of mLDs (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of LD sizes in confocal images of control and Act5C-depleted FBs.

claim: RNAi depletion of other actin isoforms did not measurably alter the average sizes of either pLD or mLD pools.
source: In contrast, RNAi depletion of the other actin isoforms did not measurably alter the average sizes of either LD pool, although there was a mild increase in average mLD size in Act57BRNAi tissues (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of LD sizes in FBs with RNAi depletion of different actin isoforms.

claim: FB-specific Act5C depletion significantly reduced larval TG levels to approximately 10% of 6-day age-matched controls.
source: Consistent with their altered LD morphologies, FB-specific Act5C depletion significantly reduced larval TG levels, which were ~10% of 6-day age-matched controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by TG measurements from whole larvae.

claim: Major de novo lipogenesis genes like ACC and FASN were expressed at normal levels in Act5CRNAi FB compared to controls.
source: Whereas major de novo lipogenesis genes like acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and fatty acid synthase (FASN) were expressed at normal levels in Act5CRNAi FB compared to controls, genes for TG production including GPAT4, the diacylglycerol acyltransferase (DGAT) enzyme MDY, and the fatty acid desaturase DESAT1 were significantly reduced in expression, suggesting a defect in TG synthesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data measuring mRNA levels of lipogenesis genes.

claim: Genes for TG production including GPAT4, MDY, and DESAT1 were significantly reduced in expression in Act5CRNAi FB.
source: Whereas major de novo lipogenesis genes like acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and fatty acid synthase (FASN) were expressed at normal levels in Act5CRNAi FB compared to controls, genes for TG production including GPAT4, the diacylglycerol acyltransferase (DGAT) enzyme MDY, and the fatty acid desaturase DESAT1 were significantly reduced in expression, suggesting a defect in TG synthesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data measuring mRNA levels of TG synthesis genes.

claim: The expression of the TG lipolysis enzyme Brummer (BMM) and mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation importer CPT1 were significantly reduced in Act5CRNAi FB.
source: The expression of the TG lipolysis enzyme Brummer (BMM), as well as mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation importer CPT1, were significantly reduced, suggesting the observed TG reduction was not a result of elevated lipolysis nor enhanced fatty acid oxidation.
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data measuring mRNA levels of lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation genes.

claim: Act5C-mutant cells displayed a disrupted cortical actin network compared to adjacent control cells.
source: As expected, Act5C-mutant cells from successful mitotic recombination (identified by loss of the RFP marker) displayed a disrupted cortical actin network when stained with phalloidin or Cell Mask compared to adjacent control cells (Figure 2F and G, red arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging of mosaic FBs with Act5C-mutant clones.

claim: Act5C-depleted cells exhibited perturbed pLD morphologies compared to adjacent control cells.
source: Notably, Act5C depleted cells also exhibited perturbed pLD morphologies compared to adjacent control cells (Figure 2G, red arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging of mosaic FBs showing LD morphology differences.

claim: LDs appeared sparser in individual Act5C-depleted cells, and a clear pLD layer was missing in the cell periphery.
source: LDs appeared sparser in individual Act5C-depleted cells (similar to general loss of Act5C in the entire FB), and a clear pLD layer was missing in the cell periphery.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging observations of mosaic FBs.

claim: Age-matched L3 Act5C-deficient larvae were undersized compared to late feeding/pre-wandering controls.
source: However, we found that age-matched L3 Act5C-deficient larvae were undersized compared to late feeding/pre-wandering controls, suggesting a developmental arrest or significant delay (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging of larvae expressing GFP in their FBs.

claim: Control larvae reached critical weight and commenced wandering and pupating between days approximately 5-6 after egg laying (AEL).
source: Consistent with this, control larvae reached critical weight, and commenced wandering and pupating between days ~5–6 after egg laying (AEL), whereas there was a significant delay in the growth of Act5C-deficient larvae (Figure 3B, and see table Supplementary file 2 for developmental details).
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental timeline observations.

claim: Act5CRNAi larvae lingered in the food for an additional 7-14 days (approximately 2-3 times slower relative to controls).
source: In fact, Act5CRNAi larvae lingered in the food for an additional 7–14 days (~2–3 x slower relative to controls), gradually increasing their overall size (taking up to 3 weeks) to nearly match controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental timeline observations.

claim: Developmentally delayed Act5CRNAi larvae appeared transparent and were lipodystrophic with small FBs compared to controls.
source: However, these developmentally delayed larvae appeared transparent, and upon imaging were lipodystrophic with small FBs compared to controls (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging of larvae.

claim: TG levels of 3 week old Act5CRNAi larvae were higher than at day 6, but still much less than L3 pre-wandering controls.
source: TG levels of these 3 week old larvae were higher than at day 6, but still much less than L3 pre-wandering controls (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by TG measurements from larvae at different developmental stages.

claim: Less than 10% of larger Act5CRNAi larvae eventually wandered and pupated, but became necrotic during metamorphosis and failed to eclose to adult flies.
source: A few larger larvae did eventually wander and pupate (<10%), but became necrotic during metamorphosis and failed to eclose to adult flies (Figure 3B, C and D, red arrows denote necrotic pupae).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations of pupal development and imaging.

claim: FBs extracted from wandering Act5CRNAi larvae showed underdeveloped tissue lobes with significantly smaller cells.
source: Indeed, FBs extracted from wandering Act5CRNAi larvae showed underdeveloped tissue lobes with significantly smaller cells, suggesting Act5C was required for normal FB development and cell size (Figure 3F, G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging and quantitative analysis of FB cell sizes.

claim: Allowing Dcg-Gal4; tub-Gal80ts X UAS-Act5CRNAi parents to lay eggs at 29°C for 1 day (embryogenesis only), then lowering to 18°C for the remainder of development, enabled larvae to successfully develop into flies.
source: First, we allowed Dcg-Gal4; tub-Gal80ts X UAS-Act5CRNAi parents to lay eggs at 29 °C, which were maintained at this non-permissive (Act5COFF) temperature through embryogenesis (i.e. 1 day). We then lowered the culturing temperature to the permissive 18 °C for the remainder of larval development to permit Act5C expression (Act5CON). Surprisingly, this 1 day Act5C depletion during embryogenesis still enabled larvae to successfully develop into flies (Figure 4A), suggesting that expression of Act5C in fat body progenitor cells was not essential for early adipogenesis or FB cell differentiation during late embryogenesis (Hoshizaki et al., 1994; Yongmei Xi, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: Act5CRNAi cultures maintained at 29°C for 2 days still successfully progressed into flies.
source: Next, we extended the Act5COFF 29 °C treatment for 2 days and 3 days, depleting Act5C during embryogenesis and through the L1 and/or L2 stages of larval development. Indeed, vials cultured at 29 °C for 2 days still successfully progressed into flies.
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: Act5CRNAi cultures maintained at 29°C for the initial 3 days began displaying varying degrees of arrested larval development and pupal necrosis.
source: However, Act5CRNAi cultures maintained at 29 °C for the initial 3 days began displaying varying degrees of arrested larval development and pupal necrosis, although some still progressed into flies, indicating Act5C may be functionally required during the post-L1 stages of larval development (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: Extending the 29°C treatment for 4 days resulted in progressively fewer larvae able to develop into flies.
source: Extending our 29 °C treatment for 4 days resulted in progressively fewer larvae able to develop into flies, and 5 days at 29 °C resulted in the developmental arrest and necrotic pupae observed with constitutive Act5C depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: When Act5CRNAi cultures were initially placed at the permissive 18°C for only 0.5 day* or 1 day*, then switched to 29°C, larvae exhibited developmental arrest and failed to generate flies.
source: Intriguingly, when cultures were initially placed at the permissive 18 °C for only 0.5 day* or 1 day*, then switched to 29 °C, larvae exhibited developmental arrest and failed to generate flies, suggesting that Act5C expression in the FB only during embryogenesis is not sufficient for complete Drosophila development (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: Extending the permissive 18°C treatment for 1.5 days* resulted in a small, but variable (≤30%) proportion of flies hatching.
source: Next, we extended the permissive 18 °C treatment for 1.5 days*, and observed a small, but variable (≤30%) proportion of flies hatching across several culture vials analyzed.
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: Extension to 2 days* at 18°C enabled approximately 70% of pupae to eclose to flies.
source: Further extension to 2 days* at 18 °C enabled ~70% of pupae to eclose to flies (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: An almost complete rescue was noted with vials maintained for 2.5 days* at 18°C.
source: An almost complete rescue was noted with vials maintained for 2.5 days* at 18 °C.
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: FBs of Dcg-Gal4 >UAS-Act5CRNAi larvae maintained at 25°C throughout development did not contain a cortical actin network.
source: Indeed, we observed that while FBs of Dcg-Gal4 >UAS-Act5CRNAi larvae maintained at 25 °C throughout development did not contain a cortical actin network (phalloidin-stained), those maintained at 18 °C exhibited a partial F-actin network, indicating some Act5C was still present at this cooler temperature (Figure 4C, red arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by phalloidin staining and confocal imaging of FBs at different temperatures.

claim: FBs of Dcg-Gal4 >UAS-Act5CRNAi larvae maintained at 18°C exhibited a partial F-actin network.
source: Indeed, we observed that while FBs of Dcg-Gal4 >UAS-Act5CRNAi larvae maintained at 25 °C throughout development did not contain a cortical actin network (phalloidin-stained), those maintained at 18 °C exhibited a partial F-actin network, indicating some Act5C was still present at this cooler temperature (Figure 4C, red arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by phalloidin staining and confocal imaging of FBs at different temperatures.

claim: Larvae constitutively maintained at 18°C were generally larger and successfully developed into flies.
source: Furthermore, larvae constitutively maintained at 18 °C were generally larger and successfully developed into flies, whereas those maintained at 25 °C exhibited developmental arrest and pupal necrosis, indicating that at 18 °C Act5C was expressing above its functional threshold (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental observations and imaging of larvae at different temperatures.

claim: Act5CRNAi larvae cultured at 18°C displayed improved FB tissue morphology and normal FB cell sizes.
source: The Act5CRNAi larvae cultured at 18 °C also displayed improved FB tissue morphology and normal FB cell sizes (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging and quantitative analysis of FB cell sizes.

claim: Maintaining Dcg-Gal4 >UAS-Act5CRNAi cultures for 1 day at 25°C, then switching to 18°C permitted full development into flies.
source: Like the Gal80ts system, maintaining cultures for 1 day at 25 °C, then switching to 18 °C permitted full development into flies (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: Extending the 25°C timeframe to 2 days still allowed fly development.
source: Extending the 25 °C timeframe to 2 days still allowed fly development, whereas 3 days at 25 °C led to developmental arrest and necrotic pupae similar to continually maintaining them at this temperature (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: 3 days at 25°C led to developmental arrest and necrotic pupae.
source: Extending the 25 °C timeframe to 2 days still allowed fly development, whereas 3 days at 25 °C led to developmental arrest and necrotic pupae similar to continually maintaining them at this temperature (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: Dcg-Gal4 >Act5CRNAi cultures kept at 18°C for only 1 day* (Act5C expressed during embryogenesis only) failed to develop into flies.
source: Like the Gal80ts system, cultures kept at 18 °C for only 1 day* (Act5C expressed during embryogenesis only) failed to develop into flies, whereas some larvae from cultures maintained at 18 °C for 1.5 days* could successfully complete metamorphosis into flies (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: Some larvae from cultures maintained at 18°C for 1.5 days* could successfully complete metamorphosis into flies.
source: Like the Gal80ts system, cultures kept at 18 °C for only 1 day* (Act5C expressed during embryogenesis only) failed to develop into flies, whereas some larvae from cultures maintained at 18 °C for 1.5 days* could successfully complete metamorphosis into flies (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: Cultures maintained for the initial 2.5 days* at 18°C completed normal development into flies.
source: Cultures maintained for the initial 2.5 days* at 18 °C completed normal development into flies, underscoring that expressing Act5C only during embryogenesis is not sufficient for full development.
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments and developmental observations.

claim: Depletion of Twinfilin (Twf) in the FB led to significantly decreased FB cell size resembling Act5C loss.
source: Indeed, depletion of Twf in the FB (Dcg-Gal4 >UAS-TwfRNAi) led to significantly decreased FB cell size resembling Act5C loss, indicating that actin dynamics are necessary in the FB for normal FB cell expansion (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of FB cell sizes in Twf-depleted FBs.

claim: Larvae from cultures kept at 18°C for the initial 1 day* or 1.5 days* accumulated significantly less TG than controls.
source: As expected, there was a direct correlation between smaller FB cells and reduced TG storage. Larvae from cultures kept at 18 °C for the initial 1 day* or 1.5 days* accumulated significantly less TG than controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by TG measurements from larvae in temperature-shift experiments.

claim: TG levels progressively increased with longer times at the permissive temperature (2 day* and 2.5 day*).
source: TG levels progressively increased with longer times at the permissive temperature, that is, 2 day* and 2.5 day* (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TG measurements from larvae in temperature-shift experiments.

claim: Loss of Act5C expression during embryogenesis only (1 day at 29°C) did not significantly impact FB cell sizes of L3 larvae.
source: Next, we examined FB cell sizes and TG levels of larvae from cultures initially maintained at the non-permissive 29 °C temperature (Act5COFF). Loss of Act5C expression during embryogenesis only (1 day at 29 °C) did not significantly impact FB cell sizes of L3 larvae, and their TG levels mirrored controls (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of FB cell sizes and TG measurements from larvae in temperature-shift experiments.

claim: Extension of the non-permissive 29°C to 3 days and 5 days caused progressive reductions in both FB cells size and TG stores.
source: However, extension of this non-permissive 29 °C to 3 days and 5 days caused progressive reductions in both FB cells size and TG stores in these larvae (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of FB cell sizes and TG measurements from larvae in temperature-shift experiments.

claim: After 1 hour of feeding, less than 1% of Act5CRNAi larvae had visible dye in their guts compared to greater than 90% of controls.
source: Following 1 hr of feeding,<1% of Act5CRNAi larvae had visible dye in their guts compared to >90% of controls (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual feeding assay observations.

claim: After 4 hours in the dyed food, approximately 20% to 40% of Act5CRNAi larvae displayed some gut dye, but dye amounts were approximately 50% reduced relative to controls.
source: However, after 4 hr in the dyed food,~20% to 40% of Act5CRNAi larvae displayed some gut dye, but even amongst those actively feeding, dye amounts were ~50% reduced relative to controls. This suggested a feeding defect in Act5CRNAi animals (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual and quantitative feeding assay data.

claim: Act5CRNAi tissues displayed an approximately 50% reduction in Target-Of-Brain-Insulin (Tobi) transcripts.
source: QPCR analysis revealed that Act5CRNAi tissues displayed a ~50% reduction in Target-Of-Brain-Insulin (Tobi) transcripts as well as a ~threefold increase in the expression of ImpL2, a DILP2 antagonist, suggesting insulin signaling was blunted in Act5C-deficient FBs (Buch and Pankratz, 2009; Lee et al., 2021, Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data measuring mRNA levels of insulin signaling genes.

claim: Act5CRNAi tissues displayed an approximately threefold increase in the expression of ImpL2, a DILP2 antagonist.
source: QPCR analysis revealed that Act5CRNAi tissues displayed a ~50% reduction in Target-Of-Brain-Insulin (Tobi) transcripts as well as a ~threefold increase in the expression of ImpL2, a DILP2 antagonist, suggesting insulin signaling was blunted in Act5C-deficient FBs (Buch and Pankratz, 2009; Lee et al., 2021, Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by QPCR data measuring mRNA levels of insulin signaling genes.

claim: Act5C-deficient FBs displayed reduced PM-localized tGPH relative to cytoplasmic and nuclear signals, indicating reduced insulin signaling.
source: Indeed, Act5C-deficient FBs displayed reduced PM-localized tGPH relative to cytoplasmic and nuclear signals, indicating reduced insulin signaling in Act5CRNAi larvae (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantification of tGPH reporter localization.

claim: Act5CRNAi larvae displayed significantly reduced DILP2 in their hemolymph compared to controls.
source: Act5CRNAi larvae displayed significantly reduced DILP2 in their hemolymph compared to controls, again indicating reduced insulin signaling (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data measuring DILP2 levels in hemolymph.

claim: The BODIPY-C12 signal in FBs from Act5CRNAi larvae was significantly higher compared to controls.
source: Intracellular BODIPY-C12 could be detected in both control and Act5C-depleted FB tissues (Figure 7A, B and C). Surprisingly, the BODIPY-C12 signal in FBs from Act5CRNAi larvae was significantly higher compared to controls, suggesting Act5C loss did not inhibit the capability of FBs to absorb extracellular lipids, and in fact Act5C loss may promote extracellular lipid absorption.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification of BODIPY-C12 uptake in FBs.

claim: 2-NBDG was at least as abundant in Act5C-depleted FB tissues as in controls.
source: 2-NBDG was dimly detected in the cytoplasm of FB cells, and appeared at least as abundant in Act5C-depleted FB tissues as in controls, suggesting Act5C loss did not reduce the ability of FB tissue to absorb extracellular carbohydrates (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification of 2-NBDG uptake in FBs.

claim: Neither hemolymph glucose nor trehalose levels were altered in Act5C-deficient larvae.
source: We monitored circulating hemolymph levels of both glucose and trehalose in control and FB-specific Act5CRNAi larvae, and surprisingly found neither was altered (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical measurements of hemolymph glucose and trehalose levels.

claim: FB glycogen levels were not significantly different between control and FB-specific Act5CRNAi larvae.
source: Next, we evaluated FB carbohydrate stores by monitoring tissue glycogen levels. Consistent with the tissue's ability to absorb circulating carbohydrates ex vivo, FB glycogen levels were not significantly different between control and FB-specific Act5CRNAi larvae (Figure 7I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical measurements and PAS staining of FB glycogen.

claim: hGlut4-GFP could be successfully trafficked to the surfaces of Act5C-deficient FB cells.
source: To further confirm that FB tissues could deliver carbohydrate transporters to the cell surface for uptake from circulation, we imaged a GFP-tagged model glucose transporter, hGlut4-GFP (Crivat et al., 2013) expressed in larval FBs using the UAS-Gal4 system. As expected, hGlut4-GFP could be successfully trafficked to the surfaces of Act5C-deficient FB cells, suggesting the transport of glucose transporters to the cell surface was not significantly impacted by Act5C loss (Figure 7K).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging of hGlut4-GFP localization in FBs.

claim: Mid-guts from larvae with FB-specific Act5C-depletion displayed significant LD accumulation.
source: Strikingly, whereas control mid-guts exhibited small sparse LDs, mid-guts from larvae with FB-specific Act5C-depletion displayed significant LD accumulation, and closely resembled larvae lacking ApoLpp (ApoLppRNAi), implying a defect in mid-gut lipid export (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging of Nile Red-stained larval guts.

claim: FB-specific TwfRNAi loss resulted in significant fat accumulation in larval mid-guts.
source: Like Act5C depletion, FB-specific TwfRNAi loss also resulted in significant fat accumulation in larval mid-guts, indicating that disrupted F-actin turnover in the FB resulted in gut fat accumulation (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging of Nile Red-stained larval guts.

claim: Both Act5C and Twf FB-depletion significantly elevated gut TG compared to controls.
source: To quantify relative gut fat accumulation, we isolated guts from these larvae and measured TG levels. Indeed, both Act5C and Twf FB-depletion significantly elevated gut TG compared to controls (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TG measurements from isolated larval guts.

claim: Act5C loss in the FB significantly reduced hemolymph DAG.
source: Consistent with defective inter-organ trafficking, Act5C loss in the FB significantly reduced hemolymph DAG (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical measurements of hemolymph DAG levels.

claim: Loss of both beta-spectrin and alpha-spectrin altered pLD sizes at the cell periphery.
source: Consistent with their role in organizing cell surface architecture that intimately associates with pLDs, loss of both beta-spectrin and alpha-spectrin altered pLD sizes at the cell periphery (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and quantitative analysis of pLD sizes in spectrin-depleted FBs.

claim: mLDs were not significantly affected by loss of beta-spectrin and alpha-spectrin.
source: However, mLDs were not significantly affected, distinct from Act5C and Twf loss (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of mLD sizes in spectrin-depleted FBs.

claim: Beta-spectrin loss in the FB did not lead to fat accumulation in the larval gut.
source: In line with this, beta-spectrin loss in the FB did not lead to fat accumulation in the larval gut (in fact, gut TG levels were actually reduced in larvae that lacked FB beta-spectrin) (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and TG measurements from larval guts.

claim: Hemolymph of beta-spectrin depleted larvae displayed normal circulating DAG levels.
source: Moreover, hemolymph of beta-spectrin depleted larvae displayed normal circulating DAG levels, indicating that loss of the FB spectrin network did not impact inter-organ lipid trafficking like Act5C loss (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical measurements of hemolymph DAG levels.

claim: F-actin still localized to FB cell-cell boundaries in beta-spectrin RNAi-depleted FBs.
source: Furthermore, we find that F-actin still localized to FB cell-cell boundaries in beta-spectrin RNAi-depleted FBs, although the FB cell surface appeared significantly less ruffled (Figure 8—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging of F-actin in beta-spectrin-depleted FBs.

claim: In control tissues, Lpp particles were concentrated in the FB cell periphery just below the cell surface.
source: Notably, in control tissues Lpp particles were concentrated in the FB cell periphery just below the cell surface (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging of Lpp in FB tissues.

claim: Lpp particles formed distinct clusters in close proximity to pLDs adjacent to the cell surface.
source: In fact, high resolution imaging indicated that Lpp particles formed distinct clusters in close proximity to pLDs adjacent to the cell surface (Figure 9A, red arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-resolution confocal imaging of Lpp and LDs.

claim: Act5CRNAi FBs displayed a bright Lpp immuno-stain throughout the tissue interior, and the Lpp signal was no longer polarized to the cell periphery near pLDs.
source: In striking contrast to controls, Act5CRNAi FBs displayed a bright Lpp immuno-stain throughout the tissue interior, and the Lpp signal was no longer polarized to the cell periphery near pLDs (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging of Lpp in Act5C-depleted FBs.

claim: In control tissues, grape-like particle clusters were observed in close proximity to some LDs that resembled Lpp fluorescence immuno-staining.
source: In control tissues, we observed grape-like particle clusters in close proximity to some LDs that resembled Lpp fluorescence immuno-staining (Figure 9B, red arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging of FB tissues.

claim: Individual Lpp-like particles were approximately 60 nm in diameter.
source: By TEM, individual particles were ~60 nm in diameter, in close agreement to the expected sizes of Lpp particles (Wojczynski et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM measurements and is consistent with published data on Lpp particle sizes.

claim: Some Lpp-like particles were observed in the microridge folds at the FB cell surface.
source: Moreover, we observed some particles in the microridge folds at the FB cell surface, indicating they may be secreted by FB cells (Figure 9C, blue stars).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging of FB tissues.

claim: Lpp-like particles were no longer observed in ApoLpp-depleted FB TEM sections.
source: To investigate whether these Lpp-like particles were in fact Lpp particles, we did TEM of ApoLpp-depleted FB TEM sections (Dcg-Gal4 >ApoLppRNAi), and found these particles were no longer observed, supporting that they were Lpp particles (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging of ApoLpp-depleted FBs.

claim: TEM of Act5CRNAi FBs revealed that the Lpp particles were no longer sequestered in grape-like clusters adjacent to LDs.
source: Strikingly, TEM of Act5CRNAi FBs revealed that the Lpp particles were no longer sequestered in grape-like clusters adjacent to LDs. Instead, these particles now appeared to accumulate inside FB cells and distributed throughout the cell interior, similar to the anti-Lpp IF signal (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM imaging of Act5C-depleted FBs.

claim: FB-specific loss of either Sar1 or Tango1 resulted in LD accumulations and TG increases in the larval gut.
source: Strikingly, FB-specific loss of either Sar1 or Tango1 and Act5C produced common defects. Both included LD accumulations and TG increases in the larval gut (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging and TG measurements from larval guts.

claim: Sar1 and Tango1 loss exhibited decreased whole-larval TG levels.
source: Sar1 and Tango1 loss also mirrored Act5C FB depletion in that they exhibited decreased whole-larval TG levels (Figure 9D), as well as lower hemolymph DAG pools (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by TG and DAG measurements from whole larvae and hemolymph.

claim: Staining for Lpp particles in Tango1-depleted FBs revealed an identical build-up of intracellular Lpp in FB cells as Act5C loss.
source: In line with this, staining for Lpp particles in Tango1-depleted FBs revealed an identical build-up of intracellular Lpp in FB cells as Act5C loss, indicating that loss of Act5C or Tango1 led to similar defects in Lpp secretion (Figure 9E, red arrows).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging of Lpp in Tango1-depleted FBs.

claim: dGRASP65-GFP foci were reduced in abundance in Act5C-depleted FBs, particularly in the mid-plane.
source: However, dGRASP65-GFP foci were reduced in abundance in Act5C-depleted FBs, particularly in the mid-plane, indicating Act5C loss impacted Golgi homeostasis in the FB.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging of dGRASP65-GFP in FBs.

claim: RNAi depletion of either Act5C or Tango1 led to reductions in secreted ApoLII in the hemolymph.
source: Indeed, RNAi depletion of either Act5C or Tango1 led to reductions in secreted ApoLII in the hemolymph, consistent with a block in Lpp release from the FB (Figure 9F).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data measuring ApoLII levels in hemolymph.

claim: General protein staining revealed reduced secreted proteins in Act5CRNAi and Tango1RNAi hemolymph.
source: Similarly, general protein staining (Ponceau stain) also revealed reduced secreted proteins in Act5CRNAi and Tango1RNAi hemolymph, indicating loss of Act5C possibly impacted secretion of other proteins and/or adipokines from the FB.
evidence: The claim is supported by Ponceau staining of hemolymph proteins.

claim: Beta-spectrin-depleted FBs showed no major defects in ApoLII and protein secretion.
source: In contrast, beta-spectrin-depleted FBs showed no major defects in ApoLII and protein secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and Ponceau staining data.

claim: Both ApoLpp and Act5C FB depletion produce analogous phenotypes such as reductions in larval FB cell size and developmental arrest.
source: In line with this, both ApoLpp and Act5C FB depletion produce analogous phenotypes such as reductions in larval FB cell size, and developmental arrest (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D, table Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of FB cell sizes and developmental observations.

claim: Drosophila actins share 98% similarity with humans.
source: Drosophila actins share 98% similarity with humans (Schroeder et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Drosophila express 6 actin isoforms: 2 cytoplasmic isoforms (Act5C and Act42A), 2 larval muscle isoforms (Act57B and Act87E), and 2 adult muscle actins (Act79B and Act88F).
source: While humans have as many as 20 actins, Drosophila express 6: 2 cytoplasmic isoforms (Act5C and Act42A), 2 larval muscle isoforms (Act57B and Act87E), and 2 adult muscle actins (Act79B and Act88F) (Burn et al., 1989; Röper et al., 2005; Wagner et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Actin isoforms are not functionally redundant.
source: Despite their close relation, actin isoforms are not functionally redundant, as substituting one for another does not always rescue the phenotype arising from the missing isoform.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about actin isoform specificity.

claim: Actin isoforms exhibit highly spatially and temporally regulated expression patterns both in tissues and across organismal development.
source: This is because these actins exhibit highly spatially and temporally regulated expression patterns both in tissues and across organismal development (Wagner et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The Drosophila larval fat body is functionally analogous to the mammalian adipose tissue and liver.
source: In Drosophila, the central metabolic organ regulating energy storage and signaling is the fat body (FB), functionally analogous to the mammalian adipose tissue and liver (Arrese and Soulages, 2010; Musselman et al., 2013; Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Adipogenesis is completed during late embryogenesis when FB cells merge into a single-cell thick continuous tissue comprising of approximately 2200 cells.
source: Adipogenesis is completed during late embryogenesis when FB cells merge into a single-cell thick continuous tissue comprising of ~2200 cells primed to store nutrients including triglycerides (TG) in lipid droplets (LDs) and excess sugars as glycogen for energy homeostasis (Bharucha, 2009; Hoshizaki et al., 1994; Yongmei Xi, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: During larval development FB cells do not increase in number, but instead expand enormously in size over a 4-5 day period.
source: During larval development FB cells do not increase in number, but instead expand enormously in size over a 4–5 day period to accommodate the TG and biomass necessary for metamorphosis (Meschi and Delanoue, 2021; Yongmei Xi, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Through three instar stages (L1-L3), feeding larvae increase approximately 200 times in overall biomass, much of which consists of FB LDs.
source: Thus, through three instar stages (L1-L3), feeding larvae increase ~200 x in overall biomass, much of which consists of FB LDs (Sriskanthadevan-Pirahas et al., 2022; Jacobs et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Critical weight (CW) is defined as the minimum threshold weight at which 50% of larvae can proceed to pupation without further feeding.
source: Defects in FB nutrient storage can result in larvae failing to reach their 'critical weight' (CW), defined as the minimum threshold weight at which 50% of larvae can proceed to pupation without further feeding (De Moed et al., 1999; Juarez-Carreño et al., 2021; Nijhout and Williams, 1974; Tennessen and Thummel, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Circulating Lpp particles receive DAG lipids from the gut, then traverse the hemolymph to deliver them to the FB for LD storage.
source: Circulating Lpp particles receive DAG lipids from the gut, then traverse the hemolymph to deliver them to the FB for LD storage.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Lpp-mediated lipid trafficking in Drosophila.

claim: Lpp particles are synthesized and secreted by FB cells.
source: Lpp particles are themselves synthesized and secreted by FB cells, and loss of FB Lpp production or secretion perturbs inter-organ nutrient flux, causing lipid accumulation in the mid-gut and developmental arrest prior to pupation (Heier et al., 2021; Matsuo et al., 2019; Palm et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of FB Lpp production or secretion perturbs inter-organ nutrient flux, causing lipid accumulation in the mid-gut and developmental arrest prior to pupation.
source: Lpp particles are themselves synthesized and secreted by FB cells, and loss of FB Lpp production or secretion perturbs inter-organ nutrient flux, causing lipid accumulation in the mid-gut and developmental arrest prior to pupation (Heier et al., 2021; Matsuo et al., 2019; Palm et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lipoprotein trafficking to the brain promotes DILP2 secretion from insulin producing cells (IPCs) and influences systemic insulin and nutrient signaling.
source: It has been shown that lipoprotein trafficking to the brain promotes DILP2 secretion from insulin producing cells (IPCs) and influences systemic insulin and nutrient signaling, although the mechanisms underlying this are still being explored (Brankatschk and Eaton, 2010; Brankatschk et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The actin network of mammalian pre-adipocytes undergoes dramatic remodeling during adipocyte differentiation.
source: For example, the actin network of mammalian pre-adipocytes undergoes dramatic remodeling during adipocyte differentiation (Hansson et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mature adipocytes accumulate F-actin at the cell surface, forming a cortical actin network together with the spectrin protein fodrin that supports the caveolae-rich surface membrane.
source: Whereas pre-adipocytes exhibit intracellular actin stress fibers, mature adipocytes accumulate F-actin at the cell surface, forming a cortical actin network together with the spectrin protein fodrin that supports the caveolae-rich surface membrane (Kanzaki and Pessin, 2002; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mice fed a high-fat diet exhibit a significant expansion of adipocyte cell size (hypertrophy) that requires cytoskeletal rearrangements to harbor fat stores.
source: Mice fed a high-fat diet also exhibit a significant expansion of adipocyte cell size (i.e. hypertrophy) that requires cytoskeletal rearrangements to harbor fat stores (Hansson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Enlarged adipocytes exhibit increased F-actin pools and elevated actin modulating factors.
source: How this rearrangement is coordinated remains enigmatic, but enlarged adipocytes exhibit increased F-actin pools and elevated actin modulating factors, suggesting lipid accumulation correlates with actin polymerization.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about adipocyte hypertrophy and actin dynamics.

claim: Adipocyte actin networks can regulate the delivery of glucose transporters like Glut4 to cell surfaces for carbohydrate uptake in mice.
source: In mice, adipocyte actin networks can regulate the delivery of glucose transporters like Glut4 to cell surfaces for carbohydrate uptake, but whether this is a general regulatory feature of actin networks in adipose tissues remains unclear (Brozinick et al., 2007; Kanzaki and Pessin, 2002; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Defective nutrient storage and adipocyte enlargement (hypertrophy) are emerging features of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes.
source: Defective nutrient storage and adipocyte enlargement (hypertrophy) are emerging features of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about metabolic diseases.

claim: Dysfunctional hypertrophy is a recognized feature of diseases such as obesity and type 2 diabetes.
source: Dysfunctional hypertrophy is a recognized feature of diseases such as obesity and type 2 diabetes, but the mechanisms governing adipocyte cell size determination and expansion remain poorly understood (Nunn et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: High-nutrient diets can drive the dramatic expansion of adipocyte cell size (hypertrophy) in mammals.
source: In mammals, high-nutrient diets can drive the dramatic expansion of adipocyte cell size, termed hypertrophy, that enables them to absorb and store elevated nutrients as fat, thus avoiding lipotoxicity and ensuring metabolic homeostasis (Hansson et al., 2019; Virtue and Vidal-Puig, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.
